title: Toilet routine
steps: Take her to your chosen spot after waking, eating, drinking and play, and frequently while awake.|Stand quietly; reward immediately after she finishes outside.|If nothing happens, return to close supervision and try again soon. Clean accidents with enzymatic cleaner; never punish.
goal: Track patterns rather than expecting a fixed bladder capacity.

title: Learning to rest
steps: Offer a toilet trip and a quiet, comfortable resting area.|Dim activity around her; reward calm briefly, then let her sleep undisturbed.|Keep the space close enough for reassurance. If restless, check discomfort, toilet needs or overstimulation rather than forcing sleep.
goal: Can relax with support between short active periods.

title: Choose the right chew
steps: Remove access to shoes, cables and unsafe objects before play.|Offer a size-appropriate chew and supervise for damage or swallowing.|Praise choosing her chew; trade for a treat if you need to remove it. Ask your vet about suitable chew hardness.
goal: Chooses safe available items in a managed space.

title: Puppy biting & redirection
steps: Keep an appropriate toy within reach during play.|If teeth contact skin, pause calmly and offer the toy. Reward choosing it.|If she keeps biting, end the interaction and use a gate for a brief calm reset; check toilet and sleep needs. Do not hold her muzzle.
goal: Can switch to a toy; play ends before overtired biting escalates.

title: Peace with her big sister
steps: Give your older dog a puppy-free resting area behind a gate. Feed separately and put prized chews away.|Let both dogs notice each other at a comfortable distance; reward calm attention separately.|Keep supervised meetings brief. Interrupt puppy pestering by redirecting Clover; separate before either dog becomes tense.
goal: Both can disengage and rest. Never leave them together unsupervised.

title: Bedroom bedtime routine
steps: Before bedtime, prepare a puppy-safe sleeping arrangement with no accessible gaps or fall routes; prevent jumping on or off a high bed. Keep her dog bed in your room ready if the shared bed cannot be made safe.|Offer a calm toilet trip immediately before settling in your bed or on her dog bed in your room, then keep activity low and let her settle close to you.|Expect overnight toilet needs. Respond to waking, sniffing or restlessness with a calm toilet trip, then return to bed. Reward toileting outside; never punish accidents.
goal: Settles comfortably with you and receives safe, responsive overnight toilet support; a full dry night is not required.

title: Relax in the downstairs pen
steps: Set up the pen beside you, with water and an open crate secured safely inside or attached; feed her separately from her sister.|After a toilet trip, reward voluntary entry, scatter part of her measured meal, and let her explore the open crate without shutting it.|Close the pen gate for a second while you remain beside her, reward calm, then reopen. Build short comfortable periods with you nearby; respond to distress by making it easier.
goal: Comfortable behind the pen gate with you nearby, able to eat or relax. Duration grows in tiny steps.

title: Crate training & safe pen
steps: Place her open crate within or attached to the downstairs pen, secured so its door cannot swing shut. Reward voluntary entry and let her leave freely.|Offer part of a meal or a safe chew inside while the crate remains open; the pen is the usual downstairs boundary.|Separately, when she is comfortable, try a one-second crate-door closure while beside her, reward and reopen. Build gradually for occasional travel or care needs. This is not her overnight sleeping arrangement.
goal: Voluntarily rests in the open crate; any brief closure remains comfortable and separate from bedtime.

title: Settle while I work in my room
steps: Puppy-proof the room: secure cables, shoes, bins, small objects and escape routes. Start after a toilet trip and short play.|Put a comfortable mat or bed beside your desk. Reward calm while you work for a few seconds, then pause for a check-in.|Build brief work blocks with active supervision and toilet breaks. Start with a smaller gated area; if you cannot watch her, switch to her prepared safe space rather than giving unchecked freedom.
goal: Can calmly explore or rest in a manageable bedroom area while you can still supervise.

title: Yes means a reward
steps: Say “yes” calmly, then immediately give a tiny treat.|Repeat five times while she is relaxed; no requested behaviour is needed yet.|Use the marker at the exact moment of a behaviour you want, followed by a reward.
goal: Looks expectantly for a reward after the marker.

title: Name & check-in
steps: Say “Clover” once in a quiet room.|When she looks toward you, say “yes” and give a tiny treat.|Repeat five times, then finish. Do not repeat her name if distracted; move closer.
goal: Looks toward you in 4 of 5 easy repetitions.

title: Brush & body handling
steps: Show the brush and reward a voluntary approach.|Touch a shoulder briefly, then reward. Build toward one gentle brush stroke.|Practice separate tiny sessions with paws, ears and chin. Stop if she withdraws; do not restrain through fear.
goal: Loose body and voluntary re-engagement after each touch.

title: Collar & harness comfort
steps: Let her look at and sniff the harness; reward curiosity.|Hold the opening so she can voluntarily put her nose through for a treat, then remove it.|Fasten briefly when comfortable, reward, and gradually build wearing time. Check fit and avoid unsupervised snag risks.
goal: Comfortable voluntarily approaching and wearing fitted equipment.

title: Tiny alone-time practice
steps: After toileting, set up a safe pen with a suitable supervised chew.|Step away for one second and return calmly before worry.|Build in seconds, varying easy repetitions. If distressed, reduce the separation; arrange company for longer absences.
goal: Comfortable repeated short separations, not endurance.

title: Prevent resource worries
steps: Feed both dogs separately and let Clover eat undisturbed.|Occasionally walk past at a comfortable distance and toss an extra tasty treat, then leave.|Trade toys instead of taking them by force. If she freezes, growls or guards, give space and consult a qualified reward-based professional.
goal: Human approach predicts something good, without testing or provoking guarding.

title: City sounds at a distance
steps: Begin indoors with very quiet traffic or elevator sounds.|Pair a few seconds with treats or play.|Stop while she is comfortable. Increase volume or proximity on another day, never both together.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Loose body, taking food, able to look away. Move away if she freezes or avoids.

title: Different people, no pressure
steps: Let Clover observe one calm person at a comfortable distance.|Pair their presence with treats or play; ask them not to reach over her.|Let her choose whether to approach. Reward checking back with you and leave before she tires.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Can see a new person without pressure to greet.

title: New surfaces
steps: Place a stable, non-slip novel surface next to familiar flooring.|Reward looking at it, then a voluntary paw or step onto it.|Let her retreat at any time. Avoid unstable, hot, sharp or slippery surfaces.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Can explore a mild new surface voluntarily.

title: Vacuum & household activity
steps: Begin with the appliance switched off at a distance; reward curiosity.|Have a helper turn it on far away for one second while you reward Clover.|Repeat only while relaxed and let her retreat. Do not move the vacuum toward her.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Comfortable at an easy distance from brief household noise.

title: Calm observation
steps: Choose one mild new sight at a distance where she stays loose-bodied.|Reward noticing it and then turning back to you; she does not need to approach.|Leave after a few good moments. Increase distance if she hides, freezes or cannot disengage.
goal: Can notice something new and recover easily.

title: Find it
steps: Place one piece of food on a clear non-slip floor while she watches.|Say “find it” and let her sniff it out.|Build to a few visible pieces on a safe surface. Keep food games separate from the older dog and account for food portions.
goal: Enjoys a short calm sniffing game.

title: Hand target
steps: Offer an open hand a few centimetres from her nose.|Mark and reward any voluntary nose touch using your other hand.|Add “touch” and vary the hand position slightly. Use it to guide her without grabbing.
goal: Touches your hand in four of five easy attempts.

title: Sit
steps: Hold a tiny treat at nose height and move it slowly upward and back a little.|As her bottom touches the floor, mark “yes” and reward. Do not push her hips.|After several easy repetitions, say “sit” just before the hand motion, then gradually reduce the lure.
goal: Offers a sit on one cue in a quiet room.

title: Lie down
steps: From a comfortable sit or stand, move a treat slowly toward the floor between her paws.|Slide it slightly forward; mark and reward when elbows touch the floor. Never pull her legs.|Add “down” once the movement is predictable; reward on the floor and release after a second.
goal: Comfortably lowers herself without physical pressure.

title: A little place to settle
steps: Put a portable mat down in a quiet room.|Mark and reward looking at or stepping onto it. Place treats on the mat.|Reward relaxed sitting or lying down; release her after a few seconds. Build duration before adding distractions.
goal: Relaxed on the mat for 30 seconds; add only a few seconds at a time.

title: Come to me
steps: In a quiet enclosed room, crouch and say “Clover, come” once.|Reward generously when she reaches you; gently touch her harness, then release to play.|Try a few steps farther away. Outdoors use a secure long line and harness; never test near traffic.
goal: Quick response in easy settings before adding distractions.

title: Trade / drop
steps: Offer a low-value toy, then show a treat near her nose.|When she releases the toy, say “yes”, give the treat and return the toy.|Add “drop” just before offering the trade once the pattern is familiar. Never chase or pry.
goal: Willing trades with easy items. Seek help for guarding.

title: All done / release cue
steps: Reward a brief sit or mat pause.|Say “okay” once, then invite her to move with you.|Keep the pause easy so she learns the word ends the exercise. Do not rely on it for traffic safety.
goal: Moves freely after the release cue.

title: Stand for care
steps: From a sit, move a treat forward at nose height until she stands.|Mark, reward and release without holding her in position.|Add “stand”, then build one second at a time for grooming and vet checks.
goal: Stands willingly for a few seconds.

title: Toothbrushing foundations
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Ask your vet about a puppy toothbrush and dog-safe toothpaste; never use human toothpaste.|Reward a chin touch, then a one-second lip lift.|Let her taste the toothpaste, then introduce a gentle single brush stroke. Build slowly and stop when she withdraws.
goal: Accepts a brief gentle tooth touch without restraint.

title: Ear checks
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Reward her for resting near you with a relaxed head.|Lift one ear flap for a second, reward and release.|Gradually look at each ear. Do not insert swabs or use cleaner unless your vet recommends it; seek care for pain, odour or discharge.
goal: Allows a brief visual ear check.

title: Nail care confidence
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Show the nail tool at a distance and reward calm interest.|Practice a brief voluntary paw touch separately; release immediately.|Introduce tool approach, then a touch without clipping. Get a demonstration from your vet or groomer before trimming; do not clip through struggle.
goal: Offers a paw comfortably with the tool nearby.

title: Chin rest & consent
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Offer your open palm under her chin and reward a voluntary brief touch.|Gradually reward one second of resting her chin in your hand.|Introduce a tiny shoulder touch while her chin rests. If she lifts her head, stop the touch and let her choose to resume.
goal: Voluntarily returns to the chin rest after a pause.

title: Vet visit rehearsal
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Practice stepping onto a non-slip low platform at home; reward and step off.|Practice brief touches to shoulder, paws and lips separately, stopping when she moves away.|Ask the clinic whether a short happy visit is possible. Bring familiar rewards and request gentle handling.
goal: Comfortable with easy handling and a brief clinic visit.

title: Happy car moments
steps: With the car parked, introduce a suitable crash-tested restraint or secured crate.|Reward calm exploration; end before discomfort.|On later days try engine on, then a very short trip with another person observing. Discuss motion sickness with your vet.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Relaxed on short trips before attempting a commute.

title: Bath setup & gentle introduction
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Introduce the dry bath area with a non-slip mat and treats.|Practice entering and leaving, then hearing water from a distance.|When comfortable, try a little lukewarm water on paws; reward and stop. Use dog-appropriate products and avoid eyes and ears.
goal: Relaxed in the bath area before a full wash.

title: Dryer sounds at a distance
steps: For the introduction, only let her notice the item or setup from a comfortable distance and pair it with a reward. Stop there if needed; completing the procedure is not today’s goal.|Start with the dryer switched off and reward looking at it.|Introduce its sound far away or at a very low level, paired with rewards.|Build proximity slowly on different days. Avoid hot air and stop at fear; ask the groomer for short familiarization visits.
goal: Can remain relaxed around quiet grooming sounds.

title: Seeing safe dogs calmly
steps: Choose a known healthy, gentle dog and ask your vet about safe settings.|Start with parallel observation at a distance; reward calm check-ins.|Keep greetings optional and very brief, then separate. Avoid unknown off-leash dogs and busy dog parks.|Keep exposure brief, at a comfortable distance and on a clean, low-risk surface. No forced greetings. Ask your vet which settings are appropriate for her vaccination status and local infection risk.
goal: Can notice another dog and disengage.

title: Leave it
steps: Hold a treat in a closed hand; let her investigate without opening it.|When she moves away, mark and reward from your other hand.|Add the cue as she disengages. Practice with safe objects; prevent access to hazards rather than testing her.
goal: Can disengage from an easy object and look to you.

title: Loose lead beginnings
steps: Clip a light lead to a comfortable harness indoors.|Reward her beside you, take one step, and reward again.|Build to a few steps. If the lead tightens, pause and invite her back; do not jerk the lead.
goal: Five relaxed steps, then a sniff break.

title: Four paws on the floor
steps: Prepare treats before approaching a calm puppy.|Reward while all four paws are on the floor, before she jumps.|If she jumps, pause attention and reward the next grounded moment. Use a gate for visitors rather than pushing her down.
goal: Can receive attention with four paws down.

title: Comfort with brief support
steps: Reward leaning comfortably against you with freedom to move away.|Place a hand gently on her side for one second, reward and release.|Build only tiny comfortable steps; never pin or restrain through fear. Ask the vet about safe handling for necessary procedures.
goal: Accepts a brief supportive touch and chooses to return.

title: Polite greetings
steps: Ask a helper to stand sideways and ignore jumping.|Reward Clover while four paws stay on the floor.|Let her choose a brief greeting, then call her back for a treat. Skip greetings when tired or worried.
goal: Can greet briefly and return attention to you.

title: Doorway manners
steps: Use a harness and lead or a secure gate as backup.|With the door closed, reward standing calmly; open it a crack and reward again.|Close gently if she rushes without trapping her. Release through together only when safe; never test beside traffic.
goal: Can pause at a slightly open door with backup protection.

title: Responding to barking
steps: First check toilet, discomfort, fear, boredom or an approaching trigger.|Reduce the trigger or add distance, then reward a quiet check-in or calm alternative.|Practice below the barking threshold next time. Do not shout, startle or use anti-bark devices.
goal: Can recover and reorient in an easier environment.

title: Gentle tug & play rules
steps: Offer a soft long toy and let her choose to grab it.|Move it gently side to side, keeping paws on the floor and avoiding neck jerks.|Pause, trade for a treat and restart as a reward. Stop before she gets overtired or teeth reach hands.
goal: Can pause and restart enjoyable play.

title: A puppy-led sniff walk
steps: Choose a vet-approved low-risk location and a comfortable harness.|Let her pause, look and sniff at her own pace; use a loose lead.|Keep the outing brief and end before fatigue. Avoid forced running, repetitive jumping and distance targets.
goal: Returns comfortable rather than exhausted.

title: Let’s go / emergency U-turn
steps: In a quiet room, say “this way” and turn with a cheerful voice.|Reward when she follows you for two or three steps.|Practice outdoors with a harness at easy distances from distractions. Turn away early before she becomes overwhelmed.
goal: Turns with you readily in easy settings.

title: Kitchen & counter boundaries
steps: Keep counters clear and use gates while food is accessible.|Reward Clover on a nearby mat while you do one easy kitchen action.|Build activity gradually and provide a safe chew away from preparation. Do not leave tempting food as a test.
goal: Can settle in a managed spot during brief food preparation.

title: Elevators & doorways
steps: Reward calm observation of an elevator from a distance.|On another repetition approach the open door, retreat and reward.|When comfortable, take one quiet ride. Keep the lead short enough for safety without tension; prevent door entrapment.
goal: Comfortable entering, riding and exiting with you.

title: Wait for a moment
steps: Ask for a comfortable sit or stand.|Pause one second, mark, reward and release with “okay”.|Increase duration a little before adding distance. Use gates and a lead for real doorway safety.
goal: Three easy seconds with relaxed posture.

title: Home-alone progression
steps: Start from successful tiny separation practice, after toileting and with a safe resting space.|Briefly leave the room or step outside and return before worry; use a camera if helpful.|Increase in small variable steps only while comfortable. Arrange care for absences beyond her current ability; consult a professional if distress persists.
goal: Calm repeated short departures before longer absences.

title: Bring a toy back
steps: Roll a toy a short distance on a safe floor.|Praise picking it up and move away invitingly so she follows.|Trade for a treat when she reaches you, then roll again. Do not chase her to recover the toy.
goal: Returns a toy a few steps willingly.

title: Scarborough office rehearsal
steps: Confirm dogs are permitted, identify a quiet spot and a safe toilet route; ask your vet about local exposure risk.|Visit at a quiet time for 5–10 minutes with mat, water, treats and cleanup supplies.|Reward settling, take a toilet break and leave early. Increase duration only after several comfortable visits.
goal: Relaxed short visits before a half-day; arrange backup care.

title: Downtown coworking rehearsal
steps: Confirm building rules and choose an off-peak visit after easy office and travel practice.|Start outside at a comfortable distance from crowds; reward calm observation.|Try a brief indoor mat session near an exit. Leave if she cannot settle, refuses food or looks worried.
goal: Comfort around people and noise. Readiness matters more than week number.

title: Skills with distractions
steps: Choose a well-practiced cue in a quiet setting.|Add one mild distraction far away and reward generously for an easy response.|Reduce distance, duration or distraction if she struggles; change only one factor at a time.
goal: Can perform an easy familiar cue around a mild distraction.

title: Adolescent refresher
steps: Return to an easy version of a familiar skill in a quiet space.|Reward generously and keep practice brief; use a lead or gates for safety.|Gradually rebuild distractions. Temporary difficulty is a reason to simplify, not punish or demand longer sessions.
goal: Reliable easy successes before raising difficulty again.
